name: Hill County

actions.title: Data Center Construction Moratorium Enacted
actions.summary: Hill County commissioners voted 3-2 to enact what appears to be the first county-level data center moratorium in Texas, pausing construction in unincorporated rural areas for one year amid noise, water, and power concerns.

actions.title: Moratorium Rescinded After $100M Developer Lawsuit
actions.summary: Hill County commissioners rescinded the moratorium less than a month after enacting it, following a $100 million lawsuit filed by a data center developer; commissioners replaced it with a voluntary developer checklist.

contextBlurb: Hill County, roughly 55 miles south of Fort Worth, passed what appears to be Texas's first county-level data center moratorium in May 2026 after residents raised alarms about a proposed 300-acre Provident Data Centers development in north Hillsboro. The moratorium was rescinded within weeks after a developer sued the county for $100 million in damages, and commissioners replaced the pause with a non-binding developer checklist. The episode illustrated the acute legal vulnerability of Texas counties, which lack general zoning authority, when they attempt to restrict data center development.

name: Hood County

actions.title: Proposed Data Center Moratorium Voted Down
actions.summary: Hood County commissioners rejected a proposed six-month moratorium on industrial development including data centers by a 3-2 vote, after a letter from state Sen. Paul Bettencourt threatened legal action and warned the county lacked statutory authority to impose such a pause.

contextBlurb: Hood County, about 40 miles southwest of Fort Worth, faced proposals for at least four large data center projects including the 2,600-acre Comanche Circle development near Tolar, which would have nine campuses totaling up to five gigawatts next to Vistra's Comanche Peak nuclear plant. Residents warned the site sits over the Upper Trinity Aquifer recharge zone and the Paluxy River watershed, projecting up to one million gallons of daily water consumption at full buildout. After hours of packed public testimony, commissioners voted the moratorium down following a last-minute letter from Sen. Bettencourt to the Texas Attorney General threatening investigation of any county that enacted such a restriction.

name: Cameron County

actions.title: Resolution Opposing Unsafe Data Center Development
actions.summary: Cameron County Commissioners Court unanimously passed a resolution opposing any data center development that fails to incorporate adequate safeguards for natural resources and residents, and formally called on the Texas Legislature to grant counties greater regulatory authority over high-impact industrial siting.

actions.title: Resolution Opposing Potable-Water Evaporative Cooling Systems
actions.summary: The Cameron County Commissioners Court also adopted a separate resolution formally opposing the use of open-loop evaporative cooling systems or other high-volume potable water consumption technologies by data centers in the county.

contextBlurb: Cameron County in deep South Texas became a focal point for data center opposition after UK developer Eneus Energy proposed a 1,785-acre, 2-gigawatt campus near Valley International Airport outside Harlingen, a project valued at over $14 billion. The county has limited direct regulatory power over projects in unincorporated areas but passed resolutions opposing unsafe development and demanding the Legislature give counties more meaningful authority. County Judge Eddie Treviño Jr. described Cameron County as one of only a handful of Texas counties actively advocating for stronger local oversight, citing serious concerns about water and electricity access in this drought-stressed, rapidly growing border region.

name: City of Harlingen

actions.title: Public Hearings Called for Proposed 120-Day Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: Harlingen City commissioners responded to intense resident pressure by calling for public hearings on a proposed 120-day moratorium on data center applications, to allow the city to study impacts on water supply, wastewater capacity, and electrical infrastructure.

actions.title: 120-Day Data Center Moratorium Enacted
actions.summary: The Harlingen City Commission voted to enact a 120-day moratorium on accepting data center development applications in order to evaluate land-use compatibility, infrastructure demands on water and electricity systems, and to update city ordinances.

contextBlurb: Harlingen, a South Texas city near the US-Mexico border, moved toward a moratorium after community activists and residents pushed back against the proposed Eneus Energy 1,785-acre data center project just outside city limits near Valley International Airport. Although no project was formally proposed within city limits, the Harlingen WaterWorks board had already signed a preliminary agreement to potentially supply 4.6 million gallons of sewer water per day to the project. Residents packed city hall, citing concerns about water supply in an already drought-stressed region, prompting commissioners to enact the 120-day pause to modernize land regulations and conduct an infrastructure impact review.

name: Hays County

actions.title: Community Opposition and Exploration of Moratorium Tools
actions.summary: Hays County and its county seat San Marcos became a statewide flashpoint for data center opposition after hundreds of residents packed a February 2026 city council meeting to oppose a proposed AI data center rezoning, which the council then denied 5-2.

contextBlurb: Hays County — home to San Marcos — emerged as one of the most visible battlegrounds in Texas's data center debate, with residents citing concerns over water, power, and residential compatibility. Data centers have been described as extremely unpopular in Hays County, driving political pressure on local officials. The county judge publicly attributed some of Gov. Abbott's mid-2026 regulatory pivot to the political heat generated by communities like Hays County ahead of the November election cycle.

name: City of San Marcos

actions.title: Rezoning for Proposed AI Data Center Denied
actions.summary: San Marcos City Council voted 5-2 to deny a rezoning application that would have allowed an AI data center to be built in the city, following an overflow crowd of residents in opposition at city hall.

actions.title: Citywide Zoning Ban on Data Centers Enacted
actions.summary: San Marcos became the first Texas city to enact a comprehensive zoning ban prohibiting data centers within city limits, using a land-use code change rather than a moratorium to try to withstand anticipated legal challenges under the state's Death Star Law.

contextBlurb: San Marcos made national headlines in early 2026 when hundreds of residents packed city hall to oppose a proposed AI data center rezoning, which the council denied. The city subsequently became the first in Texas to enact a full zoning ban on data centers, updating its land-use code rather than issuing a moratorium in an attempt to insulate the action from legal challenge under HB 2559 and the 2023 Death Star Law. State Sen. Paul Bettencourt vowed to challenge the ban, setting up a likely court test of how far Texas municipalities can go in restricting data center development.

name: City of Lockhart

actions.title: Zoning Code Updated to Restrict Data Centers to Heavy Industrial Zone
actions.summary: Lockhart City Council updated its zoning code to formally define data centers and restrict them exclusively to the heavy industrial land-use category, confining potential development to only two designated areas of the city and requiring a special use permit as an additional barrier.

contextBlurb: Lockhart, a small city in Caldwell County southeast of Austin, took a deliberately cautious approach to data center restriction by updating its zoning ordinance rather than enacting an outright ban, aiming to achieve a de facto ban-like effect without triggering costly litigation. By limiting data centers to the heavy industrial zone and adding a special use permit requirement, city officials hoped to create what one official called 'intense filtration' for any development proposals. The strategy reflects a growing playbook among smaller Texas cities that want to control data center siting but lack the legal resources to withstand a direct challenge from industry.

name: City of Fort Worth

actions.title: Proposed Comprehensive Data Center Zoning Ordinance (First of Its Kind)
actions.summary: Fort Worth's Zoning Commission voted 7-4 to recommend denial of the city's first-ever data center zoning ordinance — which proposed setbacks, industrial-zone restrictions, noise standards, screening requirements, and generator siting rules — sending it back to City Council for revision.

actions.title: Five City Council Members Call for Temporary Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: Following the zoning commission's denial, five Fort Worth council members announced plans to propose a temporary moratorium on new data center applications at the council's August 11 meeting to allow more time for regulation development and stakeholder engagement.

contextBlurb: Fort Worth is navigating one of the most complex municipal data center policy debates in Texas, driven by surging developer interest and organized community opposition from groups like Tarrant4Change and 817 Gather. The city drafted what would have been its first comprehensive data center zoning ordinance — covering setbacks, noise limits, generator placement, and water use — but the Zoning Commission rejected it in July 2026, calling for stricter protections and more deliberation time. Residents have pressed for 1-mile setbacks from homes and hospitals, and five council members subsequently moved to pursue a formal moratorium while stronger rules are crafted.
